Chapter {#} · The values and principles of the UK
Taking the Life in the UK test

British society is founded on fundamental values and principles which everyone living in the UK should respect and support. They are based on history and traditions and are protected by law, customs and expectations. There is no place in British society for extremism or intolerance.
The five fundamental principles of British life
New citizens pledge to uphold them
The whole adult population gets a say
The law applies equally to everyone
Freedom of belief, speech and choice
Of those with different faiths and beliefs
As part of the citizenship ceremony, new citizens pledge to uphold these values:

‘I will give my loyalty to the United Kingdom and respect its rights and freedoms. I will uphold its democratic values. I will observe its laws faithfully and fulfil my duties and obligations as a British citizen.’
Following from the fundamental principles are responsibilities and freedoms shared by everyone living in the UK.
If you want to be a permanent resident or citizen, you should…
respect the rights of others, including their right to their own opinions
look after yourself and your family
look after the area in which you live and the environment
a right to a fair trial
a right to join in the election of a government

Britain is described as a modern, thriving society with a long and illustrious history, whose people have been at the heart of the world’s political, scientific, industrial and cultural development, and which is proud of welcoming new migrants. Applying for permanent residence or citizenship means agreeing to accept its responsibilities and to respect the laws, values and traditions of the UK.

Becoming a permanent resident · Life in the UK
To become a permanent resident or citizen of the UK you need to speak and read English and have a good understanding of life in the UK.
Two sets of rules in the handbook
pass the Life in the UK test (written at ESOL Entry Level 3, so no separate English test), or
pass an ESOL course in English with Citizenship if your English is below Entry Level 3
pass the Life in the UK test, and
show acceptable evidence of speaking and listening in English at B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference (= ESOL Entry Level 3)
Then apply for permanent residence (settlement) or British citizenship, with the forms, evidence and fee for your circumstances.
The test questions are written at ESOL Entry Level 3, so no separate English test was needed under the 2013 rules.
People on work visas, including Tier 1 and Tier 2 of the points-based system, normally must pass the Life in the UK test to become permanent residents.
If your English is below ESOL Entry Level 3, the alternative was an ESOL course in English with Citizenship, with a test at the end.
The application form and evidence depend on your circumstances. There is a fee, which varies by application type.
Forms and fees were on the UK Border Agency website. Requirements for citizenship may change, so always check before applying.
Remember the pairing: B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference is equivalent to ESOL Entry Level 3.
